# Decoding the Intermittent P0013 on a 2014 Buick Verano

A P0013 code indicates a problem with the "B Camshaft Position Actuator Control Circuit" or, more simply, the variable valve timing (VVT) system. On the 2.4L Ecotec engine found in your 2014 Buick Verano, this means the Powertrain Control Module (PCM) cannot properly adjust the camshaft timing to maintain optimal compression and fuel efficiency. The fact that you replaced the solenoids and the light initially went off, only to return days later, suggests the root cause wasn't a simple electrical short or an open circuit in the new parts themselves.

When a diagnostic code appears intermittentlyâturning on and off between startsâit usually points to a condition that exists only under specific operating parameters rather than a permanent hardware failure. In the context of variable valve timing, the PCM expects a specific response from the camshaft actuator within a certain number of crank revolutions after ignition is engaged. If the actuator fails to move the camshaft to the target position when commanded, the code sets. If the system returns to normal operation before the drive cycle completes or if the error condition resolves itself, the light may flicker off, only to reappear once the specific threshold for the fault is met again.

Since you have already addressed the most common failure point (the solenoids), you must look at what drives them and how they interact with the mechanical system. The wiring harness connecting the VVT solenoids to the PCM is a frequent culprit in these scenarios. Over time, the plastic connectors can degrade or corrode from exposure to engine heat cycles. A loose connection might allow the circuit to work perfectly when cold but fail once the metal expands and contracts with temperature changes, creating an intermittent open or high resistance.

Another critical area to inspect is the oil pressure feed line leading directly to the VVT solenoid. The Ecotec engine relies on a specific volume of oil pressure at the correct timing to actuate the variable valve timing mechanism. If there is a restriction in the gallery feeding the solenoid, or if the solenoid's internal plunger is stuck due to sludge buildup (even with new parts installed), the actuator will not move fast enough or far enough. The PCM sees this delay as a fault and logs P0013. It is entirely possible that the old oil pressure was sufficient to clear the code temporarily, but once you restarted the car and the engine reached operating temperature, the restriction prevented the new solenoid from performing its duty cycle correctly.

You mentioned wiping the code out of the computer. While clearing codes with a scan tool is standard practice after repairs, it does not fix the underlying mechanical or electrical fault. The light will return immediately if the condition persists. However, there is a nuance regarding "pending codes" versus "confirmed codes." Some OBD-II scanners only display a code as active if the fault has been present for at least two consecutive drive cycles. If you replaced the solenoids while the car was still running or immediately after, the PCM might have recorded a single instance of failure before clearing its memory buffers. Clearing the code allows the system to reset and monitor the new components through a fresh drive cycle.

Before tearing down the engine to inspect the camshaft phasers or timing chain guides, I recommend performing a visual inspection of the oil lines for leaks or kinks. Additionally, verify that the oil level is correct; low oil pressure can mimic a solenoid failure. If the oil quality is poor or the service interval has been significantly extended, cleaning the oil gallery and ensuring fresh oil with proper viscosity is often the necessary next step before replacing expensive internal components.

If the wiring check-out and oil system verification yield no results, the issue may lie within the PCM itself, though this is statistically less common than a clogged filter or degraded connector. At that point, checking for Technical Service Bulletins (TSBs) specific to your VIN regarding VVT actuator calibration updates could provide a software-based resolution before considering hardware replacement of the entire assembly.
